questions.stem: Large-scale agricultural expansion in rural areas (SDG 2) is a mixed activity. The following are negative impacts it can cause, except
options: Driving deforestation (SDG 15)
Being among the largest users of freshwater (SDG 6)
Chemical use and land degradation (SDG 12 and 15)
Less inequality in local communities (SDG 10)
questions.explanation: Agricultural expansion improves nutrition but drives deforestation, uses most freshwater, and can lower local quality of life and widen inequality, not narrow it [M7 s8].

questions.stem: In the inverted-U curve linking per capita income to per capita material footprint, what happens after the turning point?
options: The per capita material footprint starts to fall
The per capita material footprint keeps rising with income
Per capita income falls back to zero
The footprint stays fixed at its maximum value
questions.answerText: The per capita material footprint starts to fall
questions.explanation: The curve rises to a turning point and then declines, so technology and affluence first raise the footprint and only later may decouple it [M7 s15].

questions.stem: In the nexus approach, how should a country prioritise the SDGs?
options: In the same order as the global SDG ranking
By following the priorities of the Global North
According to its local context
By choosing only the environmental goals
questions.explanation: The nexus slide states that the country prioritises SDGs depending on the local context, so there is no one-size-fits-all [M7 s21].

questions.stem: In the SDG wheel of the Food–Energy–Water nexus, which three SDGs form the inner ring (food, water and energy security)?
options: SDG 1, SDG 3 and SDG 4
SDG 12, SDG 13 and SDG 15
SDG 9, SDG 11 and SDG 17
SDG 2, SDG 6 and SDG 7
SDG 14, SDG 15 and SDG 16
questions.explanation: The inner ring holds SDG 2 (food security), SDG 6 (water security) and SDG 7 (energy security); other SDGs sit in the middle and outer rings [M7 s22].

questions.stem: Under the "Security" reason for the FEW nexus approach, the absence or crisis of any one of food, energy or water results in:
options: No effect on the other two sectors
Social instability and economic disruption
An automatic increase in SDG funding
A temporary fall in all resource prices worldwide
Immediate achievement of SDG 13
questions.explanation: Food, energy and water are fundamental for society, so a crisis in any one of them causes social instability and economic disruption [M7 s25].

options: The transfer of SDG funds from the Global North to the Global South to close financing gaps
Two SDGs reinforcing each other within one country's policy mix
The effect of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress
The overflow of surplus indicators into national reports
questions.answerText: The effect of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress
questions.explanation: A spillover is the influence of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG achievement, even while its own ranking improves [M7 s5].

questions.stem: Indonesia imports rice to meet its food needs (target 2.1). Which cross-border effect may this cause, as an example of an SDG trade-off?
options: Loss of biodiversity in the exporting country (target 15.5)
Reduced hunger in the exporting country thanks to a larger rice supply (target 2.1)
A synergy that needs no further attention
A lower material footprint in the exporting country
questions.answerText: Loss of biodiversity in the exporting country (target 15.5)
questions.explanation: Importing food can cause biodiversity loss in the exporter (target 15.5), an SDG trade-off across borders [M7 s5].

questions.stem: The 2030 Agenda says SDGs are not achieved one by one but rest on the following principles, except
options: Place-based Priority
Transformative
Universality
Indivisibility
questions.explanation: The M7 mandate is transformative, universal and indivisible; place-based priority is a feature of STI from M5, not of this mandate [M7 s6].

questions.stem: Why can traditional analysis of SDG achievement, such as country rankings or linear correlations, be misleading?
options: It covers too few countries to be statistically valid for comparison
It includes only the environmental dimension of sustainability
It always ranks Global South countries above Global North countries
It is prohibited under the 2030 Agenda and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda
It ignores interlinkages, local context, "No One Left Behind" and spillovers
questions.answerText: It ignores interlinkages, local context, "No One Left Behind" and spillovers
questions.explanation: Rankings and linear correlations oversimplify complex, interlinked goals and miss local context, No One Left Behind and spillover effects [M7 s6].

questions.stem: In the two-objective grid of SDG interlinkages, a positive change in Objective A that comes with a negative change in Objective B is called a:
options: Synergy (reinforcing)
Peripheral relation
Spillover
Trade-off (counteracting)
Nexus
questions.explanation: A trade-off is counteracting: progress on one goal delays another. A synergy has positive change in both objectives [M7 s6, s8].

questions.stem: Which policy direction follows from the idea of synergies and trade-offs among SDGs?
options: Pursue each SDG separately to avoid interference
Scale up synergies and manage or decouple trade-offs
Drop any SDG that causes a trade-off
Ignore trade-offs because they cancel out in the long run
questions.answerText: Scale up synergies and manage or decouple trade-offs
questions.explanation: Synergies accelerate SDG achievement and trade-offs need special attention, so the aim is to maximise synergies and minimise trade-offs [M7 s6].

questions.stem: In the activity classification, what is the strategic imperative for opposed activities such as coal mining or alcohol and cigarette production?
options: Scale up their positive impact
Decouple their negative impacts
Explore ways to add positive impact
Transform themselves to align with the SDG agenda
Keep current practice because their effects are insignificant
questions.answerText: Transform themselves to align with the SDG agenda
questions.explanation: Opposed activities mainly harm the SDGs, so they must transform; core activities scale, mixed ones decouple, peripheral ones explore [M7 s9].

questions.stem: Education, public health, legal activities and scientific research are examples of which type of activity, whose strategy is to increase positive impact?
options: Core activities (synergy)
Mixed activities
Opposed activities
Peripheral activities
questions.explanation: Core activities generate many positive and few negative impacts, and their strategy is to scale the positive impact [M7 s7].

questions.stem: Since 2018, China no longer accepts imported recyclables below which purity level?
questions.explanation: Recycling can cost more than new material, and China has rejected recyclables below 99% purity since 2018 [M7 s11].

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts single stream and dual stream recycling?
options: Single stream sorts by material quality at source, while dual stream mixes all materials together
Both systems give the same market value but differ only in collection cost
Single stream mixes material qualities in one container; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value
Dual stream is convenient for households but mixes and contaminates materials
questions.answerText: Single stream mixes material qualities in one container; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value
questions.explanation: Single stream is convenient but mixes qualities; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value, showing the convenience versus cost/quality trade-off [M7 s11].

questions.stem: Based on Boar et al. (2021), synergy among SDGs in the Global North includes:
options: Only one dimension, as in the Global South
Only the economic dimension of growth and trade
All three dimensions (social, economic and environmental)
Social and governance dimensions only
None; the Global North has only trade-offs among SDGs
questions.answerText: All three dimensions (social, economic and environmental)
questions.explanation: Boar et al. found Global North synergies span social, economic and environmental dimensions, while Global South synergies cover only one [M7 s17].

questions.stem: According to Boar et al. (2021), which factor reduces the impact on the environmental dimension in the Global North's SDG synergies?
options: New technology and renewable energy
Reduced international trade
Slower population growth
Top 10 and bottom 10 country rankings
questions.explanation: The slide notes that new technology and renewable energy reduce environmental-dimension impacts in the Global North [M7 s17].

flashcards.front: What is an SDG spillover? Give an example.
flashcards.back: Effect of a country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress; a country can raise its own score while pushing harm abroad. Measured with a footprint approach. Example: importing rice (target 2.1) causes biodiversity loss in the exporter (15.5); palm oil drives deforestation and poor labour conditions (SDG 8).

flashcards.front: What principles underlie SDG interlinkages, and why do rankings mislead?
flashcards.back: SDGs are not achieved one by one; the 2030 Agenda rests on being transformative, universal and indivisible, grounded in systems thinking. Interlinkages show how progress on one target affects others; implementation must be coherent and context-specific. Rankings and linear correlations ignore interlinkages, local context, No One Left Behind and spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define synergy and trade-off between SDGs, with examples.
flashcards.back: Synergy (reinforcing): action gives positive change in both objectives, e.g. clean energy (SDG 7) helping education (4) and health (3). Trade-off (counteracting): positive change in one comes with negative change in another, e.g. agriculture (SDG 2) driving deforestation (15) and water use (6). Aim: maximise synergies, minimise trade-offs.

flashcards.front: List the four activity types and the matching strategy for each.
flashcards.back: Core (synergy; many positive, few negative): scale positive impact. Mixed (significant positive and negative): decouple negatives. Opposed (mainly negative, e.g. coal mining, alcohol, tobacco): transform. Peripheral (insignificant, e.g. cultural preservation): explore ways to add positive impact.

flashcards.front: What are mixed activities? Give the two slide examples.
flashcards.back: Activities with both significant positive and negative SDG impacts. Large-scale agricultural expansion (SDG 2): feeds people but drives deforestation (15), is the largest freshwater user (6), and can widen inequality (10). Renewable energy (SDG 7): energy access but long-term trade-offs such as bird deaths, marine habitat loss, loss of fertile land (SDG 14/15).

flashcards.front: Why can recycling cost more than new material, and what is single vs dual stream?
flashcards.back: Collecting, sorting and cleaning mixed waste is costly. Since 2018 China rejects recyclables below 99% purity (Indonesia and African countries also receive them). Single stream: one container, mixed material qualities. Dual stream: sorted by quality, raising market value. Trade-off: collection convenience vs processing cost and quality.

flashcards.front: How does technology use affect SDG 12, and what does the inverted-U curve show?
flashcards.back: Development and technology use raise material and environmental footprints, hindering SDG 12 (targets 12.2 and 8.4). Inverted-U: per capita material footprint rises with per capita income until a turning point, then falls (decoupling). Examples: IKN construction materials, 12 coal power plants. This is the T of IPAT.

flashcards.front: Compare SDG synergies in the Global North and South (Boar et al. 2021).
flashcards.back: Global North: synergies include all three dimensions (social, economic, environmental); new technology and renewable energy reduce environmental impact. Global South: synergies cover only one dimension, so gains in one area often come at others' expense. North's synergies may partly rely on outsourcing impacts through spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define the nexus approach and its principles.
flashcards.back: Deepens integration between goals and targets across sectors, avoids unsustainable and inefficient conflicts and overlaps, and strengthens synergies while reducing trade-offs. Principles: ensure access to resources for vulnerable groups, promote efficient use of resources, ensure sustainability. Countries prioritise SDGs by local context.

flashcards.front: What is the Food–Energy–Water nexus and which SDGs sit at its core?
flashcards.back: Food, energy and water interact and affect the SDGs yet are often managed separately: food needs water and energy, energy needs water and land, water needs energy. Inner ring of the SDG wheel: SDG 2 (food), 6 (water), 7 (energy); managing it well ripples to all 17 SDGs.

flashcards.front: Name and group the nine reasons for a FEW nexus approach.
flashcards.back: A. Basic needs/scarcity: limited access, increasing demand, limited resources. B. Global/environmental: global goods (traded internationally), regional differences, interdependence with climate and environmental change. C. Security/governance: security (a crisis causes instability), tightly regulated markets, identification and management of risks.
